---
title: Microcontroller
description: "A board as an agent of its own: Rust without an operating system, the same App and #[action] as on a desktop, running on an ESP32 with embassy. When it is worth it, and where to start."
type: guide
---

A stage controller, a shutter, a temperature probe or a pump often sits behind a microcontroller.
Such a board can be an Arkitekt agent **itself**: it registers actions and publishes state, with
no computer in between.

It uses the same Rust crates as a desktop app, the same `App`, `#[action]` and
`#[derive(State)]`, built without the standard library and run on
[embassy](https://embassy.dev), an async runtime for bare metal.

## Use it when

- The device **has no computer** next to it, or should not depend on one.
- It is **simple**: a few actions and a little state.

If a PC is attached anyway, a [device app](/docs/build/apps/device) on that PC that talks to the
board over serial is usually easier to write and to debug.

## The shape

From the [ESP32 demo](/docs/build/embedded/first-device): an action drives a pin and publishes what
the board is now.

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Serialize, Deserialize, State)]
#[state(name = "Led")]
struct LedState {
    /// Whether the LED is on
    on: bool,
}

/// LED
///
/// Switches the board's LED on or off.
#[action]
async fn set_led(on: bool, state: StateMut<LedState>) -> anyhow::Result<bool> {
    led::set(on);                      // drive the pin
    state.set(LedState::now())?;       // publish what it is now
    Ok(state.read(|led| led.on))
}
```

The board is provisioned over Bluetooth: in Orkestrator, under **Lok → Provision a device**, you
pick it, and Orkestrator sends it the Wi-Fi credentials, the deployment's address and a key it
issues for the board. The board keeps them in flash and dials out to the server like any agent. No
port is opened on the board.

## What to watch

- **It is experimental.** The embedded stack is young and changes quickly. Do not use it for
  safety-relevant hardware.
- **State is precious here.** Every update is a frame over Wi-Fi from a small device. The demo's
  sensor hook reads the chip once a second but publishes only when a value moved by a meaningful
  step (half a degree, 3 dB), so noise never becomes a stream of updates. Do the same (see
  [Anti-patterns](/docs/build/anti-patterns#frequency)).
